product: commentary — no product. Reveals the 3-layer ad model (angle / format / execution) and the rebuild-cheapest-first method for reviving dead winners.
hook: "Most brands have a winning ad they haven't made yet and the footage is already sitting on a hard drive."
body: Every winning ad has 3 layers: angle (the emotional reason someone buys), format (UGC talking head, static, podcast clip, meme), and execution (creator, hook, script, pacing). When an ad dies it's almost never the angle — it's stale execution: the hook is tired, the audience has seen the creator's face four times. The fix is rebuilding the cheap layer while keeping the expensive proven one: old footage, new DR script, same angle — which is why it became the top spender. Rebuild order is cheapest first (truncated).
idea: Don't chase new winners from scratch — resurrect dead winners by rebuilding only the execution layer.
sequencing: Diagnosis: dead ads die from stale execution, not dead angles.
The fix: old footage plus a new DR script, same angle.
Why it works: keeps the proven expensive layer, refreshes the cheap one.
formatting: not in file (text post, no creative shown).
why_it_works: Angles are expensive to prove; execution is cheap to refresh — rebuilding preserves the proven asset instead of discarding it.
what_to_steal: Apply to LC shock-headline statics: keep the winning angle (e.g. tarnish fear), refresh only the headline execution when fatigue hits.

product: commentary — no product. Uses a parasite supplement ad as the example of scroll-stopping static hooks.
body: A lesson in static hooks: instead of generic benefit lines ("Support a healthy gut", "Feel better naturally", "Cleanse from within"), the ad leads with family betrayal. The product doesn't appear until after the curiosity gap is created; then the twist — "Because she drains parasites." It's absurd, creates an information gap, and forces reading the next line. The lesson: people don't stop scrolling because the product is interesting; they stop because they need to know what happens next — then the product inherits that attention.
idea: A shock headline opens an information gap; a twist line resolves it into the product.
sequencing: Shock headline: "My sister slept with my husband."
Twist resolves the story into the product: "Because she drains parasites."
Lesson: attention first, product inherits it.
Generic benefit lines shown as the losing alternative.
formatting: Static ad with bold headline text; two photos attached.
why_it_works: Information-gap theory — the brain cannot tolerate an unresolved story, so it keeps reading.
what_to_steal: LC shock headlines in the same mold: "MY NECKLACE TURNED MY SKIN GREEN AT MY OWN WEDDING" — then the twist into waterproof LC pieces.
